comments.text: The mayor isn't saying he's going to arrest Netanyahu, he's saying he's exploring what the law actually allows, and that's where everyone is missing the point. The legal reality is far more interesting than the headlines suggest. Yes, the mayor has no authority to arrest a sitting head of government. The U.S. isn't an ICC member, head-of-state immunity applies, and federal law preempts local action. That much is settled. But here's what everyone overlooks: the mayor has no legal obligation to protect Netanyahu either. Under U.S. constitutional law, the government has no affirmative duty to protect individuals from private violence. The mayor can simply decline to allocate NYPD resources to Netanyahu's security detail. He can refuse to coordinate with federal authorities. He can withhold the red carpet treatment entirely. That's not a crime, that's a discretionary decision. And here's where it gets legally fascinating: if diplomats from ICC member states, enjoying full diplomatic immunity under the Vienna Convention, were to take matters into their own hands and attempt to detain Netanyahu, the mayor would be legally powerless to stop them. He cannot arrest diplomats. He cannot interfere with their immunity. He can only stand aside. Some will call that looking the other way. Others might call it non-cooperation with a war criminal. But legally, it's called following the law as written. The federal government can huff and puff. They can threaten sanctions and removal. But they cannot prosecute a mayor for failing to protect a foreign leader he had no legal duty to protect in the first place. And they cannot prosecute diplomats who are immune from U.S. jurisdiction. The mayor may not be able to arrest Netanyahu, but he can make it crystal clear that if someone else with immunity chooses to act, he won't lift a finger to stop them. And that's not a threat, it's a statement of legal fact. Look, I'm not saying this is his plan. I have no inside knowledge and I'm not claiming to know what he's thinking. But if you connect the dots, this is a legally viable path that exists within the framework of the law. And if the mayor is as smart as I think he is, this is exactly the kind of avenue he's exploring. He doesn't need to break any laws or order anyone to do anything. He just needs to step aside and let the legal architecture do what it was designed to do. That's not conspiracy, that's strategy. And honestly, refusing to be an accomplice to a war criminal's protection is more than most elected officials have the courage to do.
